title: Each direction of an issuer conversion is a separate instance with its own deposit address
content:
The Paxos section holds one Instance Configuration Document per conversion direction: USDC to PYUSD, PYUSD to USDC (A.6.1.1.1.2.6.1.3.1.12.2), PYUSD to USDG (.12.3) and USDG to PYUSD (.12.4). Each names an `Asset Supplied By Spark Liquidity Layer` and a `Token to Receive`, and each carries a **different** `Paxos Deposit Address` — `0x2f7BE67e...` for PYUSD→USDC (.12.2.2.2.3), `0x227B1912...` for PYUSD→USDG (.12.3.2.2.3), `0x035b322D...` for USDG→PYUSD (.12.4.2.2.3).

The addresses are what make the routes distinguishable. On-chain, all Spark does is transfer an ERC-20 to an address; the instruction 'convert this to USDG rather than USDC' is carried entirely by *which* address receives it. Paxos infers intent from destination, so the deposit address is not a contact detail but the operative parameter of the whole conduit.

Note that PYUSD→USDC and PYUSD→USDG send the same asset from the same source to different addresses. A transposition between the two would produce a completed, valid, unreverted transfer that returns the wrong stablecoin — a failure mode with no on-chain guard, since the rate limits are keyed per instance and both would be satisfied.

Modelling direction as a first-class object is the right response: it gives each leg its own limit, its own approval and its own audit trail. It also means the count of `Active` instances overstates the count of relationships — four documents describe one commercial arrangement with one counterparty, viewed from four directions.
description: Paxos routes USDC→PYUSD, PYUSD→USDC, PYUSD→USDG and USDG→PYUSD are four documents with four distinct deposit addresses — the address, not a parameter, encodes what will be minted.
